maintopic: AGRICULTURE
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUPPORT PRICE FOR COMING YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Agricultural Stabilization Act provides for the announcement of support prices on an annual basis, and I am now announcing that the existing price basis of 44 cents a dozen for grade A large eggs delivered to Montreal will continue in effect for another 12-month period ending May 5, 1960.
The volume of eggs marketed through registered grading stations to date this year is 7 per cent more than for the same period last year. However, this does not correctly represent the actual increase because of the steadily growing movement of eggs from large-scale producers direct to retail outlets. Because of this, a greater percentage of the eggs marketed through registered grading stations is offered to the agricultural stabilization board.
From January to June, 1958 the board purchased 354,412 cases. Up to April 27 of 1959 the board had purchased 503,073 cases, and shell eggs are still being offered in unprecedented volume. With many countries of the world developing larger surpluses of shell eggs, the disposal of the surplus accumulated by the stabilization board is creating an extremely serious problem.
The continued expansion in egg production can be largely attributed to the growth in numbers and size of large commercial producers.	Because	of	integration	in thisindustry and technological developments, the present support program is providing an incentive to commercial operators to increase production. I have therefore directed the stabilization board	to	develop as	soon aspossible	a method	of	providing price support for	shell eggs	by	means of a	payment
to producers-commonly described as a deficiency payment-rather than to continue the present method of offer to purchase.
The payment to producers would be calculated on the difference between the actual market price for shell eggs for the period concerned and the prescribed support price.
This method, as in the case of the arrangement proposed with respect to hogs, would make it possible to withhold payments from commercial organizations operating under the so-called vertical integration plan, or to restrict payments to a specific volume of eggs delivered by any one producer in a given period.
I wish to assure the house that every effort will be made to have an alternative plan ready to put into operation at the earliest possible date.

The main point of the announcement is first of all, that the basic price will not be changed but that under a deficiency payment plan certain producers or commercial organizations may be barred entirely from receiving the floor price by way of a deficiency payment.
We in the C.C.F. are not opposed to this being done. In fact we are very much in favour of large commercial organizations being barred from getting their hands into the public till. speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: FOOD FOR PEACE CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to give to the house a brief report on the outcome of the food for peace conference held in Washington on May 5 and 6.
The conference was convened by the United States secretary of agriculture, Mr. Benson, and the representatives were from the five major wheat exporting countries, namely Argentina, Australia, Canada, France and the United States. The director general of the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations, Dr. B. R. Sen, was also present as a delegate.
On April 15 in the House of Commons the Prime Minister announced the calling of this conference and indicated its objectives. On several occasions in the past the Prime Minister had made suggestions for the establishment of a food bank for the assistance of countries whose populations are short of necessary food, and for long term reasons, such as the need for economic development.
The President of the United States, in his farm message to congress on January 29 of this year, made similar suggestions and subsequently instructed Mr. Benson to take the necessary steps to summon a conference to deal with the utilization of surplus food products.
The conference in the course of its two day meetings, which had been preceded by excellent preparatory work by officials of all the participating countries, suggested that the objectives in mind could best be achieved by considering projects to raise consumption of food among especially deficient groups in the population of the recipient countries; by projects to aid economic development, and by projects to establish national food reserves. There was general agreement that effective consultation was necessary for the success of any program for the utilization of surplus food products. In this way misunderstandings could be lessened and interference with commercial markets could be avoided.
Accordingly the conference agreed that a consultative committee should be set up to be composed of senior officials of the governments there represented. It was further agreed that Mr. Benson should be asked to convene the first meeting of the committee at an early date. It is expected that the meeting will be called in June.
The conference decided that the committee should, among other things, give consideration to the following:


1.	Possibilities of expanding the world's commercial trade in wheat, including the development of new markets.
2.	Ways of increasing and making more effective the utilization of wheat surpluses for the promotion of economic development and the improvement of nutritional standards.
3.	Co-ordination of disposal programs for economic development with other development activities in the recipient countries so as to ensure that such programs will contribute fully toward increasing consumption and commercial markets, and
4.	The establishment of guide lines for providing wheat to individual countries on concessional terms and the safeguarding of commercial marketings.
The conference invited Secretary Benson to convene the first meeting of the committee at an early date.
The conference resulted in a better mutual understanding among the participants of their countries' policies, problems, and proposed actions. There was discussion of the advantages of holding similar consultations on other food commodities and with other nations.
With the approval of the house I should like the communique issued in Washington yesterday to be printed as an appendix to Hansard.

speechtext:
This five nation food conference dealing with the utilization of surplus food products was called some weeks ago, and the matter with which it dealt has been under consideration by the governments concerned for a good many months. Indeed, the President of the United States made his proposal for using food for peace some months ago. Presumably, therefore, a good deal of preparation had already been made with regard to the subject before the conference held in the United States last week.
The results of the conference seem to be very inadequate, though if they do lead to any progress in dealing with this problem that progress would, of course, be welcomed. From the minister's statement it appears that the main result has been the setting up of a committee-a committee, I take it, not of ministers of the governments concerned but of officials-to keep this question under review and to exchange information with regard to it. But this subject has been kept under review by officials of the United States

and Canada for a good many years. There have also been committees set up under the auspices of the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations, and these committees have already reviewed the problems which were dealt with at this conference. If a new committee can be of any assistance it will, of course, be welcome; but this, I repeat, does not seem to be a notable result from a conference dealing with such a very important matter.
I remember the Prime Minister putting forward about a year and a half ago-and this has been echoed by other ministers-his proposal for a food bank. There is no indication from the statement the minister has just made, or from his comments, that any progress has been achieved toward the realization of that idea in practice.
The minister mentioned that Canada's position had been protected at this conference. I have in my hand a report of the conference which appeared in the New York Times of today's date by its Washington correspondent, and this correspondent points out that at the same time that the report of the conference was being issued, the United States government disclosed that it would soon expand donations and sales of wheat abroad for foreign currency in a wider effort to provide economic assistance through surplus farm products and, indeed, in a wider effort to get rid of its own surpluses. That report goes on to say-and this raises an uneasiness in our minds which is not completely dispelled by the statement of the minister-
-there was confusion about the agreement reached by the conferees. On the major point of concessional, or bargain-rate sales of wheat for foreign currencies, Mr. Benson said the other countries had "expressed willingness to make" sales. However, members of the Canadian and other delegations foresaw little possibility of such a move.
If there is that difference of interpretation and opinion already in regard to the results of this conference, I suggest to the minister it is very important to get this difference of interpretation resolved now so that this conference, inadequate though its results may have been, will at least make some progress in regard to this important matter.

maintopic: FOOD FOR PEACE CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, anything that would provide food for peace is deserving of support. There is no argument about the fact that tremendous surpluses of food are building up on the North American continent, nor is there any argument about the fact that many people in the world are hungry, but there seems to be little of a concrete nature that has come out of this conference. There has been more consultation and discussion but little action and little by way of firm agreement.
Austria State Treaty
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said that Canada's position is protected, and he spoke about our position with regard to wheat. Wheat is not the only commodity that is causing some difficulty now. As a matter of fact we are probably in a better position with regard to the disposal of wheat than we are with regard to many commodities. The Minister of Agriculture could have added other commodities including pork, eggs-after today's announcement-dairy products, large inventories of butter, large quantities of poultry meat and a possible impending surplus of turkeys. This points up the great seriousness to our economy of this ever-growing inventory in the production of agricultural commodities.
I believe in co-operation with the United States in disposing of these surpluses. I can remember when the Prime Minister was castigating the former government for undertaking special programs to dispose of their commodities. I said that a better alternative would be co-operation in the disposal of these commodities on an agreed basis.
There has been discussion but little by way of action. We suggest that there are many possibilities that should be explored and acted upon, including the acceptance of currency of other countries, the making of barter agreements, the selling of surpluses on the basis of long term contracts and the buying of goods from countries that wish to purchase our surplus produce. There are countries- Russia and Poland, to mention but two-that are anxious to buy our surpluses but because of lack of action and the inadequacy of government policy this is not being accomplished at the present time. We hope the consultations the minister has talked about will lead to action.

In my absence yesterday the hon. member for Assiniboia directed a question to the Acting Minister of Agriculture, arising out of reports with regard to the floor price for turkeys. In reply I may say there has been an exceptionally heavy increase in the marketing of turkeys. The volume marketed through registered processing plants in 1958 was 27 per cent greater than in the year earlier, and the volume marketed in the first four months of this year was 106 per cent greater than for the same period a year ago. By reason of this increase in the volume marketed there has been a progressive decline in turkey prices until they recently reached support level.
As a result the agricultural stabilization board met with representatives of the Canadian turkey federation. At this meeting numerous proposals were considered. The representatives of the Canadian turkey federation, and not the stabilization board, suggested lowering the floor price with retention of import controls. maintopic: GLENDALE AND MOUNT PEARL PARK IN METROPOLITAN AREA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, today is my second opportunity to bring the estimates of the Department of Labour and of the unemployment insurance commission before this committee. I feel that it is a privilege to do so.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: GLENDALE AND MOUNT PEARL PARK IN METROPOLITAN AREA
speechtext: Order. I wonder if hon. members would please lower their voices when they are talking to each other. It is hard to hear the member who has the floor.

maintopic: GLENDALE AND MOUNT PEARL PARK IN METROPOLITAN AREA
speechtext:
As I was saying, I feel that it is a privilege to bring these estimates before the committee. At this time I should like to

say how appreciative I am of the understanding and co-operation I have received from hon. members on all sides of this house in connection with the administration of this department. The remarks I am about to make on the estimates will be fairly general. I will try to cover every aspect of the functions of the Department of Labour and also the responsibilities that come under the unemployment insurance commission.
The estimates of the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission taken together total $90,734,240. The operations of both these departments enter into the economic and industrial streams of this country in such a way as to affect the lives of a great number of Canadians.
The unemployment insurance commission with its more than 8,000 employees, its approximately 200 offices across Canada and, of course, its great responsibility in the administration of unemployment insurance and in placement operations, is asking for $74,754,000.
The Department of Labour, with somewhat fewer than 650 employees, has responsibility for co-ordination of vocational and skilled training programs, civilian rehabilitation, women in industry, and for administration of the various federal acts governing wages, working conditions and collective bargaining and conciliation procedures. The Department of Labour is asking for a somewhat lesser amount, in the neighbourhood of $16 million.
I might just, with the permission of the committee, stress briefly the background against which these requirements are being presented. The fiscal year just past was, as hon. members know, an active one both in the fields of bargaining and of general employment. In the industrial field a number of two-year agreements came due and in the majority of cases these were satisfactorily concluded. Some proved more vexatious than others, but a final settlement was eventually reached in a great majority of these cases.
In the field of employment and placement, which applies particularly to the unemployment insurance operation, a number of positive steps were taken during the past year. It will be no news, I am sure, to hon. members when I say that we experienced a period of industrial softening in this country which I might well describe by the term "recession". Nor will it be news to them that this impinged strongly upon myself as minister in charge of the administration of unemployment insurance. Well do I recall, Mr. Chairman, the dire forebodings of certain hon. members opposite at this time last year. However, as everyone knows, the government

acted and acted quickly. The results of those actions are equally well known.
I may say that certain actions had to be undertaken at the same time in the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission. Both these departments had to be geared in line with the developing situation. Through the unanimous and wholehearted co-operation of the staffs in both departments this was done successfully.
Partly as a result of the winter work conference last year and partly as a result of suggestions from the federal-municipal conference, the municipal incentive program was developed and put into action this winter, with the result that jobs were provided for nearly 40,000 Canadians on sites where no jobs had existed before. As a result of these and other measures taken by my colleagues, employment this spring was 150,000 above last year and unemployment, according to the latest dominion bureau of statistics figures, was 72,000 lower. The administration of the municipal incentive program was largely in the hands of the Department of Labour, and this was accomplished with a minimum of complaints, so far as I know, and with no increase in staff. In short, not one single person was added to handle programs in excess of $90 million. At the same time our winter work program went ahead in much higher gear, and I would say it was far more successful than ever before.
In unemployment insurance the placement program was steadily accelerated. This effort will continue, and extra staff will be required this year on a permanent basis. This will at the same time permit the release of a number of casual employees with a consequent appreciable saving in administration costs. In unemployment insurance, which is in direct contact with a great many Canadians both for benefit and for employment purposes, the endeavour has been and will continue to be the elimination of delays and a positive emphasis on the principle of public service. All staff members are co-operating in this policy.
To come down now to the details of the estimates, the net increase this year over last, taking in supplementary estimates in both years, is of the order of some $1,113,107. This is largely accounted for by an increase of $1,300,000 in vocational training commitments to the provinces. At the same time, as I earlier pointed out, there is a decrease of $322,000 for administration in the unemployment insurance commission due to a lessening requirement for casual employees.
Perhaps I might at this point touch on some of the activities of the labour department. I think it is most important that members should grasp, at least in a general way, the
Supply-Labour
functions of this department. I sometimes fear that the impression is all too current that the minister and the department exist only to be summoned in the case of labour disputes. This is an impression which should be dispelled, since the day to day activity of the department, though it does certainly enter the field of labour conciliation, has very wide ramifications in many other aspects of industrial activity. The keeping of records, the setting of wage scales, the administration of fair wage and anti-discrimination legislation, as well as federal legislation in the collective bargaining field, the constant surveillance of the employment picture in order to anticipate future needs, the assessment of manpower requirements, the raising of the level of training skills in this country; all these are part of the very important functions of the department. They are functions which, in my estimation, are being carried out in response to a definite public need.
The role of women in industry is the responsibility of the women's bureau in my department. Recently the director acted as adviser to the Canadian government representative at the United Nations commission on the status of women. Government annuities, a form of social security for a great number of Canadians, are administered under the Department of Labour. Contracts in force number 180,000 for individuals and 247,000 group contracts. The annuity fund at March 31, 1959, stood at $1,106 million.
Conciliation of industrial disputes comes under the industrial relations branch, which in the past year has been most active indeed. Disputes numbering 108 were referred; in only six was strike action involved. Under fair wages legislation 9,000 cases were dealt with, and in October a new act, the vacations with pay act, came under the administration of this branch.
In the rehabilitation of civilians who have suffered disablement for one reason or another, new agreements with the provinces have been authorized this year, to extend a further five years. To give an example of the effect of civilian rehabilitation I might cite the case of some 2,000 persons who, before rehabilitation, were dependent upon relatives to the extent of $1,700,000 annually. After rehabilitation their earnings in the first year will total $4,660,000.
The problem of older workers is one which is receiving attention. It is receiving even more attention at this time, since it is becoming evident that a number of firms in this country have now approached the ridiculous in their attitude on this question. Recently it has been brought to my attention that certain firms are even going as low as 35 years as

Supply-Labour
the upper age limit of employment. As I have mentioned earlier, in years past this has been a problem which has touched me very deeply, and I have felt very concerned about it. Studies were recently undertaken by the economics and research branch of my department which show not only the downright fallacy but the poor economics of this position, and I hope to the able to bring these results home to employers across Canada very shortly.
I have mentioned employment and unemployment, and I think I can say that at least one thing has emerged from the events of the past year. This is that Unemployment is susceptible to a certain amount of control by direct government intervention. Let me also say, Mr. Chairman, that I am proud to be a member of a government which had the fortitude, the vigour and the vision to come to direct and positive grips with unemployment. This next winter we shall continue to wage the winter employment program with vigour.
I would pay tribute here, Mr. Chairman, to winter employment committees across Canada to the various organizations such as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, Canadian Construction Association, Canadian Labour Congress, National Council of Women and others whose support has made this effort possible. At the same time I point to the excellent co-operation we have received in connection with the municipal incentive program from provincial and municipal authorities. It has been a delight to me to have had the opportunity of being associated with this program, because of this co-operation and because of the smoothness with which it has operated.
Let me say also that studies are continuing in my department in connection with this matter of seasonal unemployment. One of the studies currently under way is being undertaken by the unemployment insurance commission in co-operation with the dominion bureau of statistics on the characteristics of the seasonally unemployed. The study was suggested in the brief of the Canadian Labour Congress to the national conference on winter unemployment, and the results cannot help but be beneficial to an understanding of this problem.
In British Columbia, where the seasonal unemployment program has assumed special and distinct characteristics, a special study is being undertaken co-operatively by the British Columbia research council, the provincial and federal governments.
One of the more important aspects of industrial development in our society is the maintenance of a high level of industrial skill.

This may in fact be the most important problem before us now. Another aspect, tying in closely with this, is the equation of the human factor with rapidly changing technological demands. I dare say that upon the manner in which we solve these two problems will depend our industrial progress in the coming 15 to 20 years. There is no need for me to emphasize to the committee at this time the vital need for maintaining a high level of industrial skill in this country, and indeed in the whole free world.
One of the measures we are taking is the technical and vocational training program now under way in co-operation with the provinces. Under agreements signed in 1957 some $40 million is being made available to the provinces over a five-year period for the establishment of suitable training facilities. Through the national vocational training advisory council such activities are co-ordinated across Canada. Another important aspect of this program is the development of uniform standards in apprenticeship training across Canada. Other aspects include training of unemployed, disabled persons and so on. Vocational guidance material is also provided to high school students across Canada.
My department is also carrying out research into skilled manpower training which will throw considerable light upon this particular problem in the years ahead. There is also a study going ahead dealing with automation and its effects upon people employed in industry which should provide results useful in the solution of a number of pressing problems. I would also mention in this connection the assistance provided by the advisory committee on professional manpower, which has been of benefit to my officials in their assessments of these problems.
All these activities are designed to assist in keeping up a high level of training skills in Canada through co-operation on the federal, provincial and industrial levels. It is essential that this co-operation be maintained, and I am hoping that as time goes on an even more intensive approach may be made to the problems in this field.
As I have said, the unemployment insurance commission is asking for $74 million. I have already pointed out the increased burden of responsibility which the commission staff faced during the past winter. Personally I do not anticipate that the effects of recession will be felt as severely in this country in the immediate future. Nevertheless I am convinced that in order to provide the type of service to which the public is entitled, the permanent staffs of the unemployment insurance offices across Canada must be supplemented. Particularly is this necessary in the placement field.

I have been stressing for some time the importance of the placement function of the unemployment insurance commission. I cannot myself, subscribe to the theory that the main function of this organization is to hand out benefits. No less important, and perhaps more so from the point of view of providing service to the taxpayer, is the necessity of an effective and positive placement program. This program will seek out jobs wherever they may be found. It will place the right person in touch with the right job. In the long run, by putting people to work rather than handing them benefits it will add greatly to the productive capacity of this country, and it will save the taxpayer money. That is why we are asking for these extra positions. At the same time the elimination of certain casual positions will result in an administrative saving in the first year of $322,000.
Hon. members will note an increase in the amount provided for office stationery. Compared to last year, and including the final supplementaries of last year, the increase is $209,000. This results partly from the extension of the mechanization program which will entail the use of special forms. Other items in the administration vote are much the same as last year.
I would point out in closing, Mr. Chairman, that during the two years of the modified recession which was felt in this country perhaps less than in any other, unemployment insurance, as administered by this government, pumped $805 million into the lifeblood of our economy. In this respect unemployment insurance became a weapon against recession, and a weapon against suffering. The balance in the fund at March 31 of this year was $496,251,386.48. At the same time last year it was $744,200,124.87.
In closing I wish to assure the members of this committee that I shall be available along with the staff of my department to answer any questions which hon. members may care to ask, and to provide any information which may be required.

maintopic: GLENDALE AND MOUNT PEARL PARK IN METROPOLITAN AREA
speechtext:
Consideration of the estimates of the Department of Labour gives members of this committee the opportunity to discuss labour and industrial problems in a general way. The committee will have listened with interest-though I think this interest was mingled with some disappointment-to the statement the minister has just made, I believe the disappointment felt by hon. members will arise not so much because of what he said as because of what he omitted to say about some of the labour problems which face us today.
Supply-Labour
If I criticize, as I propose to do, the policies of the minister and the government, the hon. gentleman will know that I have a high regard for the sincerity, the industry and the good will with which he approaches this subject. That is quite apart from the criticisms I may feel called upon to make.
I hope to deal with these matters in a general way and later some of my colleagues will discuss in more detail some of the topics the minister has just mentioned. The hon. gentleman began by making a reference to the unemployment insurance commission and the importance of its work. We all agree about its importance, especially in the months ahead. We have already had a difference of opinion in this chamber between this side and the government side concerning one matter connected with the unemployment insurance commission. Whatever side one may take in regard to the procedure followed by the government in this matter it must surely be admitted that the ultimate result of this particular appointment is unhappy and unfortunate in that the trade union representative, the workers representative on the unemployment insurance commission, one of three, has not the confidence of the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour.
To say the least, that is surely an unfortunate result. As far as I am concerned I do not believe it is genuine and effective consultation within the meaning of this particular act when a minister tells workers' organizations that a vacancy has occurred and invites them, as he did, to submit names, but also tells them that he himself is going to recommend to his colleagues in the government a particular person.
The point at issue, of course, is not the qualification of any particular person. Certainly in this case it is not that the recommendation of the government covers a man who I believe is qualified in every way to fill the post, nor is the point at issue the political views of a particular nominee, if he has any. The political views and loyalties of a government nominee or a nominee of the Canadian Labour Congress do not matter, it seems to me, if the qualifications of the nominee are satisfactory for the position and if the procedures for consultation as laid down in the act are genuinely followed.
The point at issue here, as we see it, is what constitutes this honest and effective consultation as required by the act for the purpose of ensuring-there can be no doubt but that this is the purpose of the consultation-that the workers' representative on this commission will have the confidence of the

Supply-Labour
workers' organizations as it faces-and I use the words of the minister in describing it-an increased burden of responsibility.
The minister in my view did not adequately deal with other extremely important matters, in the sense that he did not get down to principles and fundamentals in respect of at least two of the major problems that face him and that face Canada today in the field of labour, in the department over which he presides. One of those problems is that of labour-management and employee-employer relationships and the other, of course, is the problem of a continuing high level of unemployment in this country.
As far as the first problem is concerned, the minister mentioned with some satisfaction the working of the conciliation procedures of his department. No doubt he will be winding up the discussion on this item, and when that time comes I would like him to tell the committee if he will whether he feels that the present procedures of conciliation and mediation for the avoidance of wasteful and indeed anachronistic though often necessary strikes as a method of settling labour disputes are in his opinion satisfactory and adequate procedures in view of his experience in the last two years in this country. I should like him to tell us if he is satisfied as to whether these procedures are working satisfactorily in Canada at this time. If he is not satisfied, what is he doing about it and what does the government propose doing about it?
Last year when the minister opened the debate on his estimates on August 15, 1958, as reported at page 3593 of Hansard, the minister had this to say:
Coming to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, may I say that I have given notice of my readiness to consider amendments to this act and that a number of suggestions have been received and are being considered at the moment.
Perhaps the minister ten months later will bring us up to date as to the views and intentions of the government in dealing with the act and the nature of the changes that have been suggested to date. I should also like to ask the minister if he will tell the committee in due course on what principle of intervention, whether mediation or conciliation, the government acts in labour disputes, intervention by non-intervention as was the case with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation producers' strike, or intervention of the kind followed in relation to the railway diesel firemen's dispute. Also does the minister think that in the light of the problems of labour and management and the general industrial problems we are facing today the

method of protecting the public interest, which we all know is paramount, is adequate and satisfactory?
I should also like to hear the minister's views and those of the government on what can be done to reaffirm and strengthen the means of maintaining in this country the right of collective bargaining, subject always, of course, to the overriding consideration of the public interest. I believe hon. members of this committee will agree that any effort on the part of employers or of government or of anybody else to weaken that essential principle in the development of our labour relations legislation is inadmissible, just as violence and law-breaking in labour disputes is inadmissible.
Many trade unions, like corporations now have great power and efficient organization. Most of them are not the struggling groups of 50 years ago, when the right of collective bargaining was not established in this country in the way it is established now; indeed, when it was not recognized as essential by all sections of opinion as I believe it is recognized now. But along with this power, for both corporations and trade unions, must go responsibility. When that power is used irresponsibly, when there is corruption or lawbreaking, the unions themselves are the first and the greatest sufferers. I believe, and indeed it was pointed out in the debate last year by the hon. member for Skeena, that unions are the first to realize that they themselves should be the strongest guardians against that kind of thing, otherwise they would be giving ammunition to those in this country who would still like to see them weakened.
There is another problem with which perhaps the minister will be able to deal in this debate. Demands by workers for wage increases are bound to be limited and affected by economic considerations. Hence the relationship of those demands to increased productivity and to the danger of increasing costs creates a problem, thereby pushing up prices in a way which at times makes the resulting wage increase an illusory benefit.
What does the minister think of this relationship? I would like to hear his views on the most interesting proposal of one trade union-I think it was the steel workers' union -that its own demands for wage increases could be related to increased productivity in its own industry.
Of course labour, through wage demands of this kind, has its responsibility for holding back inflation which can nullify the benefits of wage increases; but perhaps there is a tendency at times to blame labour and the demands of labour too much for the effect of

increases on inflationary tendencies. There are other factors. At times we are perhaps tempted to overlook the importance of those other factors, but they are factors over which labour itself and trade unions have no control. I am thinking of the question of administered prices by corporations and groups of corporations. On this point the president of the Toronto-Dominion bank, Mr. Ashforth, had this to say on February 23 of this year, in an address before the Canadian club in Toronto. I quote one paragraph from his address:
Business, like labour, will have to make some sacrifices. It is interesting to note that corporation profits have turned buoyant again and this, of course, is a symptom of economic recovery. However, it may also be taken as evidence that management is proving fairly successful in passing on increases in costs by boosting its selling prices. It also means that business may be vulnerable to a new round of wage demands.
That, I think, Mr. Chairman, is a very wise and very significant statement, especially as coming from the president of a bank.
There is only one other particular aspect of these problems that I am going to discuss this afternoon, and that is the employment situation in this country. Last year when we debated this subject, a debate to which I have already referred, on August 15, after describing the employment and unemployment outlook for 1958 I said to the minister, and I am quoting from page 3598 of Hansard:
Perhaps he-
That is, the minister.
-will give us as clear and frank a statement as he can on this very important matter and on the policies the government intends to initiate in order to cope with what I believe to be a continuing and serious situation.
The minister replied, and I quote from page 3681 of Hansard of the same day:
In answer to that-
He was referring to my question:
-I have been advised by the officials of my department in comparing last year's conditions with the conditions this year-*
That is, 1957 with 1958.

that last year the economy was declining to a marked degree. In comparison, this year-
That is, 1958.
-the economy is on the upswing at this time.
That was in August, 1958. And he went on to say a little later on in the debate, at page 3683:
One of the best indicators is the fact that registrations at our national employment service offices were on the increase as of August last year-
That is, the increase over August, 1957.
-but we have shown that there is a steady decline week by week in the registrations at our national employment services offices in recent
Supply-Labour
weeks and although the dominion bureau of statistics figure for mid-July is not available yet-it has not been issued-I venture to predict that on the basis of the national employment service figure of 365,440 on August 7, there will be a very appreciable decrease in the D.B.S. figure for mid-July and even more so in the figure which will come out for mid-August.
The ministers optimism about the mid-July figure may have been justified by the figures as they then come out, but certainly not for the two succeeding months, I claim, Mr. Chairman, that the minister at that time took a too optimistic view of the unemployment situation in this country and that he did not at that time-though we pressed him very hard for it and we were criticized for introducing considerations of doom and gloom, as we always are when we talk about unemployment-introduce adequate policies to deal with what we thought was a continuing serious situation, and which indeed proved to be so.
When he referred to the recommendations of the conference on winter unemployment- I will have something more to say about that in a moment-which was held in mid-July, 1958 he said at page 3669 of Hansard, about a month later:
The recommendations have been made, and those recommendations are being compiled by the department for study.
That was in the middle of August. The minister went on:
I have not yet had an opportunity of presenting them to cabinet. I am going to do this because I consider this problem is very important. These matters will certainly be brought to the attention of the government for consideration.
That, Mr. Chairman, was the statement made by the minister on August 16, 1958. But not, as the minister knows-indeed, as he has already been reminded more than once until the end of October, 1958, did the government announce this offer to participate in the cost of certain municipal works designed to reduce unemployment during the winter of 1958-59. We have criticized this program, Mr. Chairman, as being too little and too late. I have already indicated in the date I have given why we considered it to have been too late.
Surely subsequent events have justified the criticism we made at that time and have repeated since. I claim, Mr. Chairman, that this program-though the minister takes a great deal of satisfaction from it-did not represent a well thought out and well planned attack on the basic problem of winter unemployment in that it was announced in October, so late that municipal authorities, without whose co-operation of course it could not have been successful at all, did not have enough notice in order to take

Supply-Labour
account of federal sharing in labour costs in preparing their own construction programs.
The program from the outset was too narrow in its conception to be of substantial aid in combating unemployment. At that time- and indeed the situation remains-certain areas had large concentrations of unemployment, and the figures show that these concentrations still exist. The successful application of this program in any such area of severe unemployment depended upon the financial resources which could be made available to the municipalities in such areas, and where such financial resources did not exist or where they were limited then the program could not operate at all, or at least could not operate to maximum effectiveness. Tying the success and the operation of the program to the financial capacity of municipalities was surely not a strong and appropriate basis for a plan that should have had as its sole basis the extent of unemployment.
When the Prime Minister announced the terms of this winter works program in his telegram of October 29, he said, and I quote from the telegram:
We believe that by co-operation these programs will create many thousands additional jobs this winter in Canada.

Although in our view the minister underestimated the seriousness of this problem in the last session, in the present session, some months later, with the facts before him, he has recognized that unemployment last year was unusually high. He has followed the example of the Minister of Finance in adopting this course. Last year in his budget speech, and later in August, the Minister of Finance said unemployment was declining, and he took a great deal of satisfaction out of that. Of course, we all did. Then, he drew the conclusion, and the minister supported him in this conclusion, that we were over the hump, through the woods, and everything was going to be much better this year. This year the Minister of Finance is again very optimistic about employment opportunities for 1959, just as he was last year in regard to employment opportunities in 1958. Then, of course, it will be too late to do anything about it. We say that the unemployed in 1959 want jobs now. 12.000	less than in February and 72,000 fewer than in March last year.

As a matter of fact, the labour force increased by only 1,000 in March in comparison with January 1959.
While it is true, and we rejoice in this, that general economic conditions have improved recently, the fact remains that the recent decline in unemployment is not due so much to that improvement as to the unusual decline in the labour force, while our population continues to increase rapidly. If that is true, that would mean about 5 per cent of our labour force, on the average, would be unemployed in 1959. Compared to the 3.1 per cent in 1956, surely that represents an extremely serious situation throughout 1959 but especially, as we enter the winter of 1959-60. It is not easy to comtemplate the possibility-and I hope the possibility will not arise-that we may, if we are not careful and if policies are not put forward to prevent it, and if our economic conditions do not improve sufficiently, be entering into a period when we will have something like a hard core of

Supply-Labour
unemployment of about that figure. I am sure that is not a prospect that any hon. member of this house contemplates with any satisfaction at all.
We feel that the government approached this problem last year by inadequate measures put into effect too late. So we ask now what are the government's intentions and policies for this year. We do not know but I think we have the right to know. Surely the provinces and the municipalities should know without delay what the government is prepared to do, what the government is planning to do for next year. It is time now to plan, to discuss, to arrive at concrete decisions. It will be too late next fall to do very much about it.
Is it the intention of the government to participate in the cost of certain municipal works next winter? If so, should not the minister announce that decision immediately? Is the minister-and to be fair to him I think he gave some indication that he was doing this in his statement this afternoon- examining last winter's program with a view to seeing how it can be improved, how its shortcomings can be removed so that it will be more effective next winter if the government participates in a similar type of program.
Would it not be highly desirable to call another meeting with the provinces and representatives of the municipalities-call it without delay, not next October, not next September but now-in order to review the winter works program in the light of last year's experience. I feel perfectly certain that the municipalities, in the light of that experience, would have some extremely helpful suggestions to make to the government as to the timing and the scope of that program as well as to their view of the degree of participation of the federal government in it. Hence I repeat that this meeting should be called immediately. I hope the minister will have something to say on this particular matter in the course of the present debate. I am content that with adequate advance planning and the effective co-operation between the provinces and the municipalities a great deal could and should be done to reduce seasonal unemployment which has been such an extremely serious problem, especially during the last two years. We have always had it in this country and I suppose we shall always have a measure of seasonal unemployment because we cannot, at least as yet, alter our climate. But the magnitude of that problem has been greater in the last two years than it was previously.
As we move on the road of economic recovery-and we all hope we are moving on

that road-we can, I suppose, expect what the economists call cyclical unemployment to decline. But we will realize, surely, that a hard core of unemployment still exists, not only because of the climate but because of the action of certain structural factors, as the economists call them. Even if we enjoy intense prosperity in the next two years- and I hope we do so-we will still have this structural unemployment, if steps are not taken to prevent it, due to technological progress and automation and to an unfavourable economic climate in certain depressed areas in this country, as we may perhaps almost refer to them. There is one other aspect of the unemployment problem which should receive the careful attention of the government, and I hope the minister will have something to say about this matter as well. Mr. Chairman, I have listened to the remarks of the Minister of Labour with great interest. The Leader of the Opposition said that the minister is a most genial person, a most disarming person, and I think some of his colleagues will agree with those remarks. We all hope that we will expedite this matter and bring the session to an early conclusion.
I was disappointed that the Minister of Labour, in his statement this afternoon was not able to assure the Canadian workers that the central problem of unemployment was being tackled and would be solved. No matter the amount of soft soap, there is little comfort in the fact that 525,000 persons are without jobs and seeking work, according to the joint release of April 21, 1959 of the Department of Labour and the dominion bureau of statistics. We face a serious unemployment crisis in Canada at the present time. There may have been some small improvement in recent weeks, but it is still a very serious crisis. The Canadian people did not expect to have this problem with them at this time. They were led to believe by the Conservative party that they had a program which would solve the question of unemployment. The Canadian people were assured that this government had a policy, and in the pamphlet entitled "Labour" which they issued during

Supply-Labour
the recent election campaign, the first words on the opening page are:
Labour: Progressive Conservative Policy. We will:
1. Maintain full employment and the highest possible standard of living.
That commitment has been broken. We are a long distance from full employment. We are a long distance from the highest possible standard of living. The Minister of Labour in introducing his estimates this afternoon has outlined no program to deal with the half million unemployed in the country at the present time. In the recent election campaign much was said about unemployment. The Prime Minister spoke on this subject at almost every meeting. He spoke about it on television, and on March 4, 1958 in a Toronto telecast he had this to say, as reported in the Montreal Star of March 5:
As long as I am Prime Minister, this government will not rest while one Canadian remains out of work. No one will be allowed to suffer.
Does the Minister of Labour say that no one is suffering today because of unemployment? Is that the position he takes? The Prime Minister spoke about this subject many times. In Halifax on March 24, with the election campaign drawing to a close, the Prime Minister had this to say: He said that his government-
-was launching "one of the greatest public works programs this country has ever seen" in order to stimulate employment. "I am able to tell you that we're over the peak as the result of our policies. I can see the light ahead-"
He was just getting the vision.
"-and employment reasonable and complete, over the next few months."
On March 24, 1958 the Prime Minister was seeing the light. He was being shown the vision of employment "reasonable and complete" within the next few months. Over one year later we are facing a great unemployment crisis in this country that the government has not solved and is not dealing with in an effective manner. The Prime Minister went on:
"I know what unemployment is. They don't have to tell me secondhand," he added. "But as long as I am Prime Minister, deficit or no deficit, no man or woman is going to be allowed to suffer because of unemployment."
With more than half a million unemployed the government reduces the deficit, but still no program to deal with this crisis. The Minister of Labour spoke in glowing terms of the government's winter works program, and it has been of some benefit. As the hon. minister pointed out, it is a demonstration that the provincial governments of this country and the federal government are able to co-operate on specific projects of value to

the nation to put people to work. But how many people have been put to work? The minister says over 40,000. That is a commendable effort. But surely that is not the thing that should be concerning the minister in the main, the accomplishment of putting
40,000	to work when half a million are out of work. This is just a flea bite compared to the major effort which is needed.
The government last year held a conference. The conference was itself delayed and the report of the conference was delayed. We asked for its report many times; we expected that when published it would be a substantial report including specific proposals. What we were given at that time was merely a record of the words spoken at the conference. We shall have, next winter, I am certain, a difficult unemployment situation. We are facing a difficult unemployment situation even now, with summer at hand. And still the government has no program for dealing with this crisis.
The Leader of the Opposition said his party has a program, and he quoted his program. The Conservative party, does not lack a program either. What could be a better program than full employment? What could be a better program than employment at a reasonable level, no one being allowed to suffer? The fact is that the financial interests which dominate the thinking and actions of this Conservative party, just as they dominate the thinking and action of the official opposition, are not prepared for government action and government intervention to the degree necessary to provide full employment in this country.

It is very easy for members of parliament to be taken in by the hysterical campaign that is being directed against organized labour at this time. It really amounts to a smear campaign. According to reports one reads in the newspapers it would seem that organized labour-your friends and mine, your neighbours and mine-are a greater menace today than communism. I see in the newspapers today far more complimentary statements about Premier Khrushchev than about organized labour in Canada. I think that is a damnable and disgraceful attitude. I believe that organized labour is an extremely important part of democracy. I believe that the right of people to associate themselves together in an industry to bargain with their employer is something all of us should protect and cherish. I do not think it results in great conflict in the industry or in a breakdown of our economy. I believe it has the opposite effect of maintaining and increasing productivity.
If we read the newspaper, listen to the radio or observe television we would be led to conclude that half of the workers in the country are striking all the time. Let ten people go out on strike somewhere and that is national news which is hysterically shouted across the country. The Labour Gazette of February 27, 1959 sets out the facts at page 190, as follows:
There were 260 work stoppages arising from industrial disputes in 1958 compared with 245 in 1957; time loss was somewhat higher and more workers were involved in 1958 than in 1957, according to a preliminary summary of strikes and lockouts released last month.
Let us see what that amounts to? I continue:
The 260 work stoppages in 1958 involved 107,497 workers and a time loss of 2,879,120 man-working days. -the time lost in 1958 amounted to 0.24 per cent of the estimated working time-
That is all; less than J of 1 per cent. On the assumption that a person who was on strike worked a 40-hour week this would mean that on the average, day in and day out, in all the strikes that were on in 1958, there were just 1,440 persons on strike. That is the great news, the source of complaint. The fact that one-half million people in Canada are unemployed apparently is a much smaller problem and considerably less newsworthy than the fact that a few hundred people were out on strike.

It is a strange thing, but we have had this particular question up in the last couple of weeks. I will quote from the constitution of the I.L.O. to prove that the Leader of the Opposition is wrong and that this is a government appointment in agreement with organized labour.
My own union is not affiliated with the Canadian congress, although there are many workers in my constituency who are. Recently there have been delegates appointed to the I.L.O. coal committee meeting at Geneva. The procedure followed in the appointment of these delegates is that the Minister of Labour is required, according to I.L.O. regulations, to consult with the Canadian Labour Congress, which is the largest representative group of labour in the country, who in turn appoint these delegates to go to the meeting.
The practice followed in the United States by the A. F. of L. and C.I.O. is that they turn over these appointments to the united mine workers. The point I should like to bring out here is the attitude of the C.L.C. on appointments. Rather than turn over the appointment of delegates to the largest group of coal miners in the country, the C.L.C. saw fit to appoint a couple of their own men to attend this conference in Geneva. I should like to read the paragraph of the I.L.O. regulations under which these appointments are made. It reads:
The members undertake to nominate non-government delegates and advisers chosen in agreement with the industrial organizations, if such organizations exist, which are most representative of employers or work-people, as the case may be, in their respective countries.

I know that certainly in my own labour union I could not qualify for committee work if I did not have a certain attendance record at my own local union. The situation is the same in my own union back home. We will always have our Bankses, our Hoffas and our Dolhantegs. In case you do not know who Dolhanteg is, Mr. Chairman, I may say that he is an officer in my own local back home. I could expound on his attitude on unions here for hours and tell you a few things about what this man's attitude is on unions. But because they are elected representatives of unions, it does not necessarily mean that they are at all times voicing the opinions of the union or of labour. I am quite well aware of how these labour conventions operate. It will be extremely interesting to observe how many fellows within the next number of years will be put up to run against Mr. Jodoin and to see how democratically he handles his labour congress in that regard. It will be interesting to see how many men can rise up in the ranks of labour.
Speaking of rising in the ranks of labour, may I say it is a shame what happened. Just about a year ago the automobile workers were up from Windsor; there was a delegation. They had a committee there which spoke for Canada. The hon. member for Essex East was present that day but he did not expound too much on his theories of labour that day, as I recall it. These men were here. It was clearly evident that among them there were delegates who could very well speak for the ranks of labour and do so more effectively than any Stanley Knowles, any Donald Maclnnis, or any other member of parliament, especially when dealing with their own particular problems. Why should Stanley Knowles be taken in the back door of the Canadian Labour Congress over and above such people who have spent their lifetime working in the interests of labour? Why should he be shoved in there? They need men like Stanley Knowles to talk for them. But at the same time, among their own men there are any number who can do a better

job of talking than can the same Mr. Knowles. At least, when they talk, they talk with sincerity, something which I doubt very much he has when it comes to labour.
This idea of criticizing the appointment of Mr. MacArthur was carried just a little bit too far, in my opinion, in view of the fact that his qualifications for such a job were outstanding. As for members associated or affiliated with the labour congress resigning, that is just another way of lying down. I feel that these fellows should stand behind the fact that they have already been appointed, should look after the interests of labour and should not resign because the game is not going to be played according to their rules. The fact that the Minister of Labour does consult with the congress does not necessarily mean, as has been pointed out in this chamber several times, that he is going to take without question recommendations put forward by them. It must be understood that the Canadian Labour Congress which I understand has a strength of over a million men, still does not represent the entire working force in this country.
Before resuming my seat I should like once again to say, now that the hon. member for Essex East is in his seat, that the answer I received with regard to the appointment of Hal Banks as a representative of Canadian workers to the conference in Geneva was anything but proper. Again I repeat that it was a most shameful thing to have any government appoint a man who represented American gangsters to represent Canadian workers.

Mr. Chairman, during the debate on the budget, I referred to certain newspaper headlines which might be used in writing the story of the present Conservative administration. In some of those headlines there was reference to a deficit unequalled in this country's history; in others, to unprecedented taxation.
In yesterday's edition of La Presse, I found still another headline which might also help write the story of this Conservative government. Indeed, in its issue, of yesterday, May 6, La Presse had a heading which ran:
Worker's unemployment insurance contributions are going up.
The item then went on to say, among other things:
Amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act just introduced by the cabinet in the House of Commons, will result in increasing the worker's contribution without increasing the weekly benefits of the insured.
Thus in the case of a man earning $51 a week the insurance premium will be 72 cents instead of

the present 56 cents. The weekly benefit, however, will remain at $21 for the single man, and $30 for the man with dependents. The increased contribution applies to all workers.
During the budget debate, the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) did no end of juggling with words. He toyed with them so much that the people of Canada had the impression that the government was not raising taxes very much on small salaries.
Well, Mr. Chairman, in the light of the report I just quoted, and of what happened yesterday in this house, we can see that, beyond the shadow of a doubt, this government has indirectly increased the taxes that will be paid by the small wage earner.
During the last two elections, we were told that the Conservative government would cut down taxes and government expenditures too. What happened since the Conservative party came into power is exactly the opposite. Present conditions further subtantiate my argument: The small wage earner is being, as I said, indirectly taxed, and workers who will be paying increased contributions to the unemployment insurance fund will not be getting increased benefits. It is even stated, in the schedule of contributions which will have to be paid by small wage earners that a person who gets a wage as little as $9 a week will have to pay in an extra dime a week into the unemployment insurance fund.
That, sir, is this government's achievement. I mention this just by the way and my purpose in rising today is to put before the house a plan which has been dear to me for many years.
For the last three years, Mr. Chairman, I have had put on the order paper a resolution designed to help people of 45 years or more, who want to find a job. I should like to quote this resolution which I put on the order paper on January 15 last, and which, I am afraid, will not be discussed during this session:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing, during the current session of Parliament, legislation that would facilitate the employment, in federal works, undertakings or businesses, as defined in section 2 of chapter 38 of the Statutes of Canada, 1956, or in any corporation set up to perform some function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada, of male or female persons over 45 years of age who, on account of their age, find it difficult to secure proper employment at the present time.
It is most imperative, Mr. Chairman, that the federal government urgently introduce some bill to stop a discrimination which is

Supply-Labour
sowing discontent and raising a problem which is already extremely serious and is growing increasingly so in Canada.
Obviously, Mr. Chairman, if such legislation were passed by parliament, it would fall short of its full effect until a similar one was passed by the various provincial legislatures.
As I suggested during the budget debate, a federal-provincial conference should be called as soon as possible in order to settle many issues concerning the central government and the various legislatures. And those issues should include the matter I am again submitting this afternoon. It is a matter of the utmost significance, Mr. Chairman, and should be settled at the very earliest opportunity.
In a question that went on the order paper some time ago, I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), how many people 45 years old and over were at that time looking for work. The answer I got was that, for the week ending January 19, 1959, there were 143,000 such people, i.e. about 35 per cent of all people then unemployed. As I mentioned, the problem of those people 45 or over who are being refused jobs because of their age must be settled without delay.
You can imagine, sir, the anxiety, the distress of a man with dependents, a man in the prime of life who, though only 45, 50 or 55 years old, has all kinds of trouble finding a job because of his age. Imagine fathers who need employment to support their family and provide for their children's education and who, at a time when they need it most, cannot find any work, and are being discriminated against because of their age. Imagine those jobless men with dependents, wandering from plant to plant, from office to office, trying to find a job and earn an honest living for their families. A man 45, 50 or 55 is still well able to support his family, and wants nothing so much as a chance to do so. But there is discrimination I just referred to which constitutes a crying injustice toward a large sector of the population of this country.
I have had occasion in recent years, to discuss the matter in this house; and as a result of my representations, I have received many letters from people in that category, describing their plight. I should like to quote from some of those letters.
On August 19, 1958, I received a letter from a citizen in Longueuil who says in part:

Dear Sir:
I had a job with the Canadian Pratt & Whitney Engines, in Longueuil. I was told that, when over 45 we were laid off, and I went a long way in order to find another job; I was always turned away, too old even at 40. Mr. Rouleau, we will have to wait for the old-age pension or operate a blind-pig in order to make a living.
I am sure the person who wrote me that letter will not operate a blind-pig in the constituency of Longueuil, because that riding is well represented. But, when a person writes a letter of that kind to say he will have to resort to dishonest means to make a living because he cannot find a job any more, I think it is an indication that the problem is really serious and must be considered and solved as soon as possible.

Among the letters sent to me, there were really pathetic cases, and it is with tears in my eyes that I read them. That is why, Mr. Chairman, I would ask the government to do its utmost to check this social unrest.

The premier of Ontario pointed out that situation, not very long ago, and stated the problem had to be solved. Well, as premier, he should have introduced some legislation to solve it at least in so far as Ontario is concerned. On the national plane, it is up to the federal parliament, in the first place, to introduce the type of legislation I have just referred to.

Mr. Chairman, if we keep on with this discrimination, there will be more and more social unrest. What would happen if we set an age limit to people seeking public office, to those who strive to get themselves elected in the various fields of public endeavour, either here in the Canadian parliament, or in the provincial legislatures, or in municipal councils? We would be deprived of people of ability, of men who can render services to the country, if an age limit of 45 were set for those who seek public office. First of all, we would be deprived of the services of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), and thus the Canadian people would not know what is a Conservative administration such as the one we now have. Thus the Canadian people would be deprived of the services of great statesmen who are anxious to serve the Canadian nation. Half the membership of the house, and more, and half the membership of provincial legislatures, would be ruled out, and thus we would lose the precious contribution of able men.
It has never occurred to anyone, Mr. Chairman, to set an age limit on those seeking public office. So why set an age limit in the field of business? Such a discriminatory practice is contrary to human dignity, and we have a duty, as members of the federal parliament, just as members of the provincial legislatures have a duty, to find some solution to this serious source of social unrest. To achieve this, as I was suggesting, the matter should be discussed at a federal-provincial conference.

legislation, an employer is forbidden to mention, in classified ads published in daily and weekly newspapers, and in radio or television broadcasts, such a requirement as "aged from 21 to 35". It is also illegal to require that an applicant be under 45.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset of my remarks let me assure hon. members of the committee that I do not intend to review the past today. I wish, however, to place before the committee a few thoughts with regard to labour in my constituency.
For many years labour in Canada was suppressed by big business. During the twenties and thirties people were pushed out of their jobs. After the war labour completely organized and became a very powerful group in the country. Today we have what might be called two sectors of the labour movement, the group of business people in management and the group of union leaders, jockeying for position, I believe they are using the rank and file members of the unions for gain.
I should like to discuss today the demerits of the new political party the wedding of which has been announced and is to take place shortly. I do not feel that the rank and file people in the unions want this merger to occur. Mr. Knowles in talking about the new political party indicated that it would represent the workers, farmers and similar groups of people across the country. May I point out that the Conservative party already does that. Our membership comprises a miner from the east coast, a fisherman from the east coast, people in various occupations and trades from the west coast and people from all walks of life and a variety of ethnic, cultural and social backgrounds. Some members of this party came from homes that knew poverty during the depression and had

Supply-Labour
to rely on charity to see them through. We are by no means the people of the big business interests, the people who are scheming to control the economy of Canada. The people who are scheming in this way are the Stanley Knowleses of today. People who think in that way have lost the farm support and so they cannot become a truly national party. My understanding is that even within the little group of eight in this house there is a great deal of dissension about the methods whereby the new political party may come into being. Surely a man like Stanley Knowles who could not even plan his own election could not plan the economy of the country as a whole.
I suspect that at the convention of the Canadian Labour Congress in Winnipeg last year a group of barefaced politicians tried to sneak in the back door and take over. It has been said that we should not have United States control of our industry; we should not have Wall street control of our finanical structure. Our defence program is developed in Washington and when it comes to external affairs we have to consult with the secretary of state of the United States. controlled unions and there are many in Canada which are completely run, democratically operated and every penny of the dues paid by members in Canada is spent in Canada. I am partial to that approach to things.
I should like to illustrate to the committee if I may one particular union with which I am familiar. I think this union can set a criterion or a pattern to be followed by quite a number of unions. It is an international union with offices and locals in the United States. I refer to the international woodworkers of America. This particular union -and it is not an isolated case; there are many like it-is completely autonomous in Canada. The international officers have no authority to come into any local union, to come into any district council or any subdivision in Canada unless they are invited there by the Canadian officers elected by the membership in Canada. That state of affairs has been in existence for quite a number of years. Every penny in dues that is paid by members to the I.W.A. in Canada is banked and spent in Canada for international purposes or district purposes or for what have you, but every penny is spent in Canada.
The officers of that particular union are elected by secret ballot of all of the membership. The constitution is amended in the same way. Every six months the local union that I was attached to, and others in British Columbia, had an audit of their accounts, of their books by a firm of chartered accountants. Griffiths and Griffiths was the firm. Every six months that chartered accountants' audit was submitted to the membership, to every sublocal. Every member of the organization had access to it. It is completely democratically run, completely membership controlled, and there is a close liaison between the question of authority and responsibility. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, this is a pattern for some other unions to follow in so far as autonomy is concerned and in so far as democratic membership control of trade unions is concerned. It does not matter whether unions have their head offices in Cincinnati or Portland or Montreal or Ottawa; it does not matter whether it is an international union or not an international union, but there may be incorrect things that creep into the organization.
